phonemes.desc: Labial-velar approximant [w], written wynn (ƿ) in the manuscripts — plain and voiced, as in modern English 'water'.
Short close front rounded [y], the vowel English later unrounded and lost: shape the lips for 'oo' while saying 'ee' — German ü in 'über', French u in 'tu'.
Alveolar trill or tap [r], fully sounded — Old English r is never silent, and here it closes the syllable hard.
Voiced alveolar stop [d], final and released — the word ends on a consonant, not a vowel's fading.

pronunciation.approximation: 'WÜRD' — one syllable: begin as in 'we', round the lips tight for ü, roll into a sounded r, and stop on d; a German speaker can say it as the start of 'Würde'.

kin.label: Old English
kin.form: wyrd, a feminine noun — 'that which happens, fate, destiny' — personified in verse and prose from the earliest records onward.

kin.label: Anglo-Saxon Futhorc
kin.form: ᚹᚣᚱᛞ (w-ȳ-r-d), the runic row of pre-Viking England; the word itself is unattested in surviving inscriptions.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Urðr, the exact cognate — eldest of the three Norns who lay down laws beneath Yggdrasill.

kin.label: Modern English
kin.form: weird — the noun of fate worn down to an adjective of strangeness by way of the prophetic 'weird sisters'.

pronunciation.note: Wyrd is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old English form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The word's thousand-year career vastly outruns its orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Fate, Destiny
domains.subtitle: The Word That Becomes What Happens
domains.lead: Wyrd is the Old English word for what happens — fate, destiny, the shape of events — built on the verb weorðan, 'to become'. It is not a goddess enthroned at a spindle but a noun the poets kept reaching for: 'Wyrd bið ful ārǣd', says the Wanderer — fate is wholly fixed. Beowulf goes to the dragon with 'Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo sceal' on his lips — fate goes always as she must. Its exact Norse cognate is Urðr, eldest of the three Norns at the well beneath the world-tree; its modern descendant is the word 'weird', the fateful worn smooth into the strange.

cards.name: The Word for Becoming
cards.desc: From weorðan 'to become': wyrd names the event itself before it names any power behind it — fate as a process, not a person, in the earliest English we have.

cards.name: Fate Goes as She Must
cards.desc: Beowulf's maxim on the threshold of every fight — 'Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo sceal' — the bravest resignation in English verse, spoken by a man who fights anyway.

cards.name: The Fixed Decree
cards.desc: 'Wyrd bið ful ārǣd' — the Wanderer's five-word verdict that fate is wholly resolved: the hardest consolation the Exeter Book offers its exiles.

cards.name: The Northern Sister
cards.desc: Urðr at the well with Verðandi and Skuld, laying down laws beneath Yggdrasill — the Old English word's exact Norse twin, personified where England kept her a noun.

symbols.name: The decree (wyrda gesceaft)
symbols.meaning: The Wanderer's 'shaping of fates' that turns the world under heaven — fate as ordinance written into things, not accident

symbols.name: The fixed resolve (ful ārǣd)
symbols.meaning: 'Fate is wholly determined' — the exile's hardest consolation, five words that close every appeal

symbols.name: The spared undoomed man (unfǣgne eorl)
symbols.meaning: Beowulf's exception — fate often preserves the man not doomed when his courage avails: the loophole that makes heroism rational

symbols.name: The wheel declined
symbols.meaning: Alfred's Boethius keeps the word wyrd but strips Fortune's wheel — fate re-founded as God's instrument, not a spinning goddess

symbols.name: The well of Urðr
symbols.meaning: The northern mirror — the norn at the spring beneath Yggdrasill where the Æsir hold their judgements

mythology.lead: Wyrd has no mythology in the usual sense — no birth, no hall, no marriage — because Wyrd is not a figure but the Old English word for fate itself. What it has instead is a dossier of sentences: the moments where the poets reach for the word and the whole Anglo-Saxon theory of destiny shows through. Four witnesses matter most — the Wanderer, Beowulf, the proverb poems, and Alfred's Boethius — and one northern mirror, the norn Urðr.

myths.title: Fate Is Wholly Fixed
myths.text:
The Exeter Book's exile opens his elegy with the coldest sentence in Old English: 'Wyrd bið ful ārǣd' — fate is wholly fixed, fully resolved, past all appeal. He has buried his lord, crossed the winter seas, and found no hall that will take him in; the word wyrd is the name he gives the weight of all of it. Near the poem's end the word returns in its grandest frame: 'eall is earfoðlīc eorþan rīce, onwendeð wyrda gesceaft weoruld under heofonum' — all is full of hardship in the earthly kingdom; the decree of fates turns the world under heaven.

Note what the poem does not do: it gives Wyrd no face, no spindle, no shrine. The word stays a noun of process — the way things go — and the poem's consolation is not that Wyrd can be moved but that God alone is the fastness that stands when her turning is done.

myths.title: Fate Goes as She Must
myths.text:
Beowulf speaks the word at every threshold. Before Grendel he commits the night to it: 'Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo sceal' — fate goes always as she must. Surfacing from the mere's edge of disaster he states the exception that governs his whole career: 'Wyrd oft nereð unfǣgne eorl, þonne his ellen dēah' — fate often spares the undoomed man, when his courage avails. The two sentences together are the poem's whole theology: doom is real for the doomed (fǣge), but for the undoomed, courage and fate divide the work.

When the dragon comes, the old king feels the balance tip: he knows himself fǣge, and wyrd no longer negotiates. The poet's grammar is exact — fate is spoken of as 'she' (hīo), grammatically feminine, half-personified by the pronoun alone, yet never once given a name, a household, or a cult.

myths.title: Fate Is Strongest
myths.text:
The proverb tradition keeps the word's power in its bluntest form. Maxims II, the catalogue of how things are, ranks her first among forces: 'Wyrd byð swīðost' — fate is strongest — ahead of winter's cold and spring's frost. The dialogue of Solomon and Saturn gives Saturn the matching proverb: fate is hard to turn, and neither wealth nor kinship can turn her.

These are the word's working senses — what the farmers and homilists meant when the poets were not listening: the unalterable course of what happens, stronger than every other thing the maxims catalogue.

myths.title: The Christian Taming of Wyrd
myths.text:
When King Alfred's circle translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy into Old English, they had to decide what to do with Fortuna and her wheel. They kept the native word: wyrd translates Fortuna throughout — but the translation is a conquest, not a courtesy. Alfred's text subordinates her absolutely: wyrd is God's work and God's instrument, the name for his providence as it is felt from below, turning the world the way a wheelwright turns a wheel — while the nave, God himself, stands still.

It is the great re-founding of the word: the pagan noun of unalterable event is retained, baptized, and set to work inside a Christian providence. Every later English use of wyrd and weird lives downstream of this translation.

myths.title: The Northern Sister
myths.text:
The Old Norse cognate is not a common noun but a name: Urðr, 'what has become', eldest of the three Norns. Völuspá sets the scene beneath Yggdrasill, where the well stands under the tree: thence come three maidens, deep in wisdom — Urðr one is called, Verðandi the second, Skuld the third. They laid down laws, they allotted life to the children of men, fates to be told. Snorri adds the daily rite: the Norns draw water from Urðr's well and pour it with the clay over the tree's roots, so its branches do not wither.

England kept the word a noun; Iceland made it a person. The two traditions preserve one inheritance in two grammars — and the PuniCodex lexicon files Wyrd under the Norse pantheon precisely for this kinship, the English word recorded in Beowulf answering its sister at the well.

lore.syncretism: Wyrd's learned afterlife begins as translation. Bosworth–Toller record the word glossing Latin fatum, fortuna, and even the Parcae — the three spinning Fates — and Alfred's Boethius makes the equation systematic, putting the English word in Fortuna's place while denying her Fortune's independence. The comparison with the Greek Moirai is therefore as old as the word's manuscript life, but Timmer's classic study sounds the necessary caution: Old English wyrd is fundamentally the event-word, 'what happens', and its personification is grammatical and poetic, never cultic — no spindle, no altar, no priesthood is attested. The honest alignment is structural: with the Norns, who in Völuspá 'laid down laws and allotted life', and above all with [[urdr|Urðr]] herself, the exact cognate, the past tense of becoming enthroned beside Verðandi and Skuld. Within the corpus the related figures are the well's company: [[urdr|Urðr]], [[verdandi|Verðandi]], [[skuld|Skuld]], and the tree they tend, [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]].
lore.culturalLegacy: The word's modern career is the strangest semantic journey in English. In medieval Scots and northern usage 'weird' stayed a noun of fate — to 'dree one's weird' is to endure one's destiny — and the prophetic women of Holinshed's chronicle were 'the weird sisters, that is (as ye would say) the goddesses of destinie'. Shakespeare took the phrase into Macbeth, the sisters' supernatural strangeness rubbed off on the word, and by the nineteenth century 'weird' meant simply uncanny, then merely odd: the noun of absolute fate worn down to an adjective of mild strangeness. Modern fantasy and gaming revived 'wyrd' as a deliberate archaism for deep fate; runic revivalism added the so-called 'wyrd rune', a blank stone invented in the 1980s with no medieval attestation — a modern ornament the inscriptions do not know. Through all of it the old word keeps its dignity in the Exeter Book and Beowulf, where it still means what it meant: what happens, wholly fixed, and faced with courage.
lore.extendedMeditation: Wyrd is the rare fate-word that never pretends to be a person. The Greeks spun fate into three women with shears; the Icelanders gave her a name and a well; the English kept her a common noun — the shape of what happens, grammatically feminine by accident of declension, addressed by no prayer and moved by no sacrifice. And yet the Beowulf poet finds the loophole that keeps the word honest: fate often spares the undoomed man when his courage avails. Doom is real, but it is not everything; between the fixed decree and the falling sword there is a space the size of a man's ellen, his courage, and in that space the whole heroic ethic of the poem lives. The Wanderer ends where Alfred ends: the decree turns the world under heaven, and the one fastness is not in the turning but above it. A word for fate that leaves room for courage and for God — that is the Anglo-Saxon settlement, and no tradition stated it more economically.
lore.originalScriptNote: The manuscripts write the word in Latin letters with wynn: ƿyrd; normalized Old English orthography prints it wyrd. In the Anglo-Saxon futhorc the word would have been carved ᚹᚣᚱᛞ (w-ȳ-r-d) — a normalized reconstruction, since no runic inscription of the word survives. Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: wyrd.com lies outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Beowulf, ll. 455 ('Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo sceal') and 572–573 ('Wyrd oft nereð unfǣgne eorl, þonne his ellen dēah') — Klaeber's Beowulf, 4th ed., ed. Fulk, Bjork & Niles (Toronto, 2008)

lore.archaeology: Wyrd is a word of manuscripts, not monuments: no runic inscription carves it, no amulet invokes it, and no material image can be identified with a personified Wyrd. Its witnesses are codices. The Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, written c. 975) preserves The Wanderer and Maxims II; the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, c. 1000, scorched in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731) alone preserves Beowulf; the Vercelli Book and the Corpus and CCCC manuscripts carry the homiletic prose where wyrd is debated. The Anglo-Saxon futhorc is itself materially attested — the ninth-century Thames scramasax bears the full inscribed row — and in that row the word would run ᚹᚣᚱᛞ (w-ȳ-r-d), though no surviving carving spells it. The manuscript hand's wynn (ƿ), borrowed from the runes into the book alphabet, is the last material trace of the runic world inside the word's own spelling.
